paragraphs.text:
By the same author: A discourse to those who mourn for those who are moving from the present life to the eternal one.

Some people treat the inevitable course of our nature as a disaster when others leave this life, and grieve bitterly for those who move from life here to the life of the mind, which has no body. Such people, it seems to me, have not considered what our life really is. Instead they share the condition of the many, who out of some irrational habit love whatever is present to them as though it were good, whatever it may be. Yet anyone placed above irrational nature by reason and understanding should lean toward only one thing: what appears good and worth choosing when reason judges it. He should not simply choose whatever seems pleasant and agreeable to him out of habit and some undiscerning attachment. So it seems right to me to find some way of drawing these people away from their attachment to what is familiar, and of leading them over, as far as possible, to a better way of thinking, one that befits rational people. In this way the irrationality about the passions that the many cultivate might be banished from human life. Our argument would take its proper course toward the subject before us if we first examined what the truly good is, then considered what is distinctive about life in the body, and finally set what is laid up for us in hope side by side with the things of the present and compared them. The inquiry would then advance toward the aim of this discourse, so that the minds of the many might be moved from the familiar to the good. All human beings have a natural attachment to the good, and every choice moves toward it, holding up the good as the goal of everything it strives for in life. For this reason, failure to discern what is really good usually produces most of our sins. If the truly good were plain to everyone, we would never have missed Him whose nature is goodness, nor would we willingly have plunged into the experience of evil,

unless things had been painted over with a false appearance of the good. So before anything else, let us work out by reason what the truly good is, so that error about it may never lead us to pursue the worse in place of the better. I say, then, that our argument must first lay down something like a definition and distinguishing mark of what we are looking for, so that our grasp of the good may be secure. What, then, is the mark of true goodness? It is not useful only in relation to something else. It does not seem beneficial at some times and useless at others. It is not good for one person and not good for another. Rather, it is good in itself, by its own nature, and it is equally good for everyone and at all times. This, at least in my judgment, is the unerring and unfailing mark by which the good is judged. For what is good neither for all, nor always, nor in itself apart from the

[?] to the majority. Even the sun itself, one would find, is good to those who share in it neither for everyone, nor always, nor in every respect. There are cases where it becomes very harmful: it blazes beyond its proper measure and dries out excessively whatever lies under it; it often brings on diseases; it worsens the illness of eyes that are already inflamed; and by rotting moisture it breeds harmful and loathsome creatures in the decay of what has spoiled. So, as has been said, out of all things we must choose as good only what is always and for everyone alike seen to have the nature of the good, which is always such and does not change with outward circumstances. Then there are the other things that seem good to people out of some rather irrational prejudice: I mean bodily and external things such as strength, beauty, noble birth, wealth, power, fame and everything of that kind. Since these are plain to everyone at first sight, I think we should pass over them in silence and not clutter the argument needlessly with what everyone agrees on. For who does not know how quickly beauty and strength pass away, how easily power is overturned, how insubstantial glory is, or how vain is people's attachment to riches? Because of their bright colour and rarity, people have supposed that the good lies in certain kinds of matter. With these distinctions drawn, we should next consider the present life, I mean this life carried on through the flesh, and ask whether it is such that it can be seen to bear the mark

of the good, or whether it is otherwise. Whatever reason finds about it will surely guide the minds of those who have looked into the matter on how we ought to regard the departure from this world. The life of our body, then, is a filling and an emptying carried on in two ways: one through eating and drinking, the other through drawing in and breathing out air. Without these, life in the flesh cannot exist. A person stops living when the alternation of these opposites no longer troubles his nature. After that, all such activity ceases completely. Nothing from outside flows into the dead or passes out of them. The body made up of these elements is separated and dissolved into the elements akin to it, and from then on nature rests in quiet, having laid to rest what is akin and of the same kind with each element: the earthy with the earth, what belongs to the air with the air, what belongs to the moist with the moist, and what corresponds to the hot with the hot. The mass made up of unlike things is no longer bound together by force and compulsion. Each of the things in us returns freely to its own home, and from then on nature ceases to hold the union of alien things together within itself by force. If anyone includes sleep and waking in the pattern of this life, along with what has been mentioned, he will not stray from the truth. For through these too nature labours, always being dragged toward opposites: now relaxed by sleep, now braced again by waking, and by both it is made ready to be emptied and filled. If, then, filling and emptying are the distinctive property of our life, it would be well now to test the mark of the good that we stated earlier against these properties of life, so as to see whether this life is the true good or something other than it. That filling in itself could not reasonably be judged to have the nature of the good is clear to everyone, because its opposite, I mean being emptied, is also thought to be good. When two things stand opposed to each other as contraries, the definition of the good cannot fit both equally. If one is good by its own nature, its opposite must surely be bad. Yet here nature draws benefit equally from each. So neither filling nor emptying can properly receive the definition of the good, and filling has therefore been shown to be something other than the good. Everyone agrees that such a thing is not desirable for everyone, nor always, nor in every form. Not only is it deadly to have one's fill of harmful things; even with suitable things, going beyond what is useful through excess often causes danger and ruin. And if, when an overfull state calls for emptying, some further excess is loaded on top of it, the result is a heap of evils that goes on to incurable illnesses. So filling is not good for everyone or in every case. Its usefulness depends on what it serves, on the time, and on quantity and quality.

In the same way one would find that its opposite, I mean emptying, is dangerous to those who undergo it if it goes beyond what is useful through excess. Yet again it is not without benefit when it serves something beneficial, provided the right time, quantity and quality are taken into account. Since, then, the form of this life we live does not match the mark of the good, it follows from what has been said that leaving such a life means being separated from nothing good. Clearly the truly, properly and primarily good is neither emptying nor filling. These have been shown to be useful at certain times, for certain purposes and in certain cases, and so the mark of what is truly good does not belong to them. Now the truly good stands opposed to what is not truly good, and there is no middle ground between the two. It follows that for those who are separated from what is not truly good, we should believe that their departure from here is toward what is good by nature. That good is good always, for everyone and in every way: not at certain times, not in certain cases, not for some purpose, but always the same and unchanging. To this good, then, the human soul passes over from life in the flesh, taking up another state of life in place of the present one. While we are mixed with flesh, it is impossible for us to see exactly what that state is. But by subtracting what we know in this life, we can form some conjecture by analogy. The soul will no longer be entangled with the grossness of the body, nor live amid the balance of opposing elements, whose evenly matched struggle with one another produces our constitution and our health. An excess or a deficiency of any of these opposites becomes an affliction and a sickness of nature. In that life nothing shrinks as it is emptied or suffers as it is overloaded. The soul is entirely beyond the discomforts of the air, I mean cold and heat, and free from everything conceived in terms of opposites. It comes to be where life is free and released from all necessary toil. It does not suffer the hardships of farming, nor endure labours on the sea, nor disgrace itself in the huckstering of trade. Separated from building and weaving and the drudgery of the menial crafts, it leads a calm and quiet life, as Paul says. It does not fight on horseback or at sea, nor grapple hand to hand in the infantry line. It is not busy making weapons, nor collecting taxes, nor building ditches and walls, but is exempt and free from all such things. It neither suffers trouble nor causes it. There slavery and lordship, poverty, noble and low birth, private obscurity and official power, and every such inequality have no place. That life lacks nothing and is free of matter, and this removes the need for all these things and their like. In it what sustains the soul's existence is not a share in anything dry or moist, but the contemplation of the divine nature; and in place of the breath of air,

we do not doubt that it is communion with the true and Holy Spirit. The enjoyment of these does not alternate between having and lacking, taking in and expelling, as in this life. It is always being filled, yet satiety never sets a limit to its fullness. For the delight of the mind weighs nothing, and it is never sated, always flooding insatiably over the desires of those who share in it. That is why that life is blessed and pure: it is no longer led astray by the pleasures of the senses in judging the good. What, then, is gloomy about the matter, that we should be downcast at the departure of those dear to us? Unless someone thinks it grievous that they depart to the life free of passion and trouble. That life admits no pain from blows. It fears no threat of fire, no wounds from iron, no calamities from earthquakes, shipwrecks or captivity, no attacks from flesh-eating beasts, no stings or bites from creeping and venomous creatures. In it no one is puffed up with pride or trampled in lowliness, made savage by boldness or cowed by cowardice. No one swells with anger, boiling with rage and raving, or is shaken by fear, unable to resist the onslaught of someone stronger. In it there is no worry about the character of kings, what the laws are, what sort of people hold office, what the decrees say, or how much the annual tax will be. No one worries whether heavy rain has fallen and flooded the farmland with its excess, whether hail has ruined the farmers' hopes, or whether a lasting drought is drying up every growing thing. That life is entirely immune from the other evils of life as well. The gloom of being orphaned does not grieve it, and the ills of widowhood have no place there. The many kinds of bodily sickness have ceased, along with envy of the prosperous and contempt for the unfortunate, and all such things are banished from that life. Equal freedom of speech and equality before the law, with complete and peaceful liberty, govern the commonwealth of souls, and each has whatever he has prepared for himself by his own choice. If, through some folly, someone has prepared something worse for himself instead of something better, death is not to blame for it, since his own choice freely took what seemed good to it. Why, then, are those who mourn the departed so aggrieved? Indeed, if someone who has shaken off pleasure and pain together with the body were entirely clean of every passionate disposition, he would have more reason to mourn those left behind. They are in the same condition as people who live in prison, whom familiarity with gloom and long acquaintance with darkness have led to think their present state pleasant and painless. Perhaps such prisoners are even downcast when others are released, not knowing the brightness that awaits those freed from the darkness. If they knew the sights of the open air, the beauty of the sky, the height of heaven, the rays of the heavenly lights, the dance of the stars, the circuits of the sun, the course of the moon, and the varied

beauty of the earth in its plants, the sweet sight of the sea gleaming smooth and rippling gracefully under a gentle breeze, and the beauty of the buildings in cities, private and public, with which splendid and wealthy cities are adorned—if those confined in prison knew these things and their like, they would not lament those led out of prison as though they were parted from something good. Rather, those outside the prison would naturally think of those still shut in as toiling in a pitiable life. So too, it seems to me, those who have left the prison of this life, if they could at all show their sympathy for the suffering by tears, would mourn and weep for anyone stretched out in the pains of this life, because he does not see the beauties above the world and beyond matter: the thrones and principalities, powers and dominions, the angelic hosts and assemblies, the city above, and the festival above the heavens of those whose names are enrolled. For the beauty that surpasses these, which the truthful word declared the pure in heart would see, is beyond all hope and higher than any guess we can make. The departed would think this alone worthy of groans and grief on our account; they would also grieve that although so many pains surround life, people have grown so attached to wretched things that they do not bear their assaults as some necessary service, but take pains to make them last forever. The desire for power, for more than one's share, and for these self-indulgent gluttonies, and for whatever else of the kind is pursued—for whose sake there are weapons and wars and mutual slaughter, and all the misery and treachery people willingly commit—is nothing but a heap of calamities brought into life by choice, with eagerness and zeal. But the departed feel no impulse to tears, since they feel no passion at all. Being mind and spirit, freed from flesh and blood, they cannot by nature be seen by [?] those buried in the grossness of the body, nor can they themselves admonish people to give up their mistaken judgment about what is real. So let our own mind speak for them. Going outside our bodies in thought, as far as we can, and drawing the soul away from its attachment to matter, let us say: "O man, everyone who shares this nature, attend to yourself, as Moses commands. Know yourself exactly, who you are. Distinguish in your reasoning what you truly are from what is seen around you, so that you never look at what is outside you and think you are seeing yourself. Learn from the great Paul, who examined our nature exactly. He says that there is an outer man in us and an inner man, and that while the one is wasting away, the other is being renewed. So do not look at the one that is wasting away and think you are seeing yourself. For

that outer man too will one day be free from corruption, when in the regeneration what is mortal and easily dissolved is refashioned into what is immortal and indissoluble. But for now, what appears of us outwardly flows away, falls apart and perishes. So we should not look at it, since it is not right to look at anything else that can be seen either. As Paul said, we look not at the things that are seen, for the things that are seen are temporary, but the things that are unseen are eternal. Instead we should turn our contemplation to what is invisible in us, and believe that we truly are that which escapes the grasp of the senses

Let us become, then, as the proverb puts it, judges of ourselves. For knowing oneself cleanses one from the faults that come from ignorance. But someone who wants to see himself cannot easily do so unless some device makes the impossible possible for us. Nature has made our bodily eyes so that they see everything else but remain unseen by themselves. In the same way the soul searches out everything else, busily examining and tracking down what lies outside it, but cannot see itself. So let the soul copy what happens with the eyes. Since the eyes have no natural power to turn their sight back on themselves and see themselves, they look at the form and shape of their own circle in a mirror and see themselves through the image. In the same way the soul must look at its own image and regard whatever it sees in the likeness it was made to resemble as its own. But we must change the illustration slightly so that the idea fits the argument. In the case of a reflection in a mirror, the image is shaped after the original. In the case of the soul's likeness, we understand the reverse, for the soul's form is made as an image of the divine beauty. So when the soul looks at its original, then it sees itself exactly. What, then, is the Divine, to which the soul has been made like? It is not body, not shape, not form, not size, not solidity, not weight, not place, not time, nor anything else of the kind by which the material creation is known. When all these and their like are taken away, what remains must surely be conceived as something intellectual, immaterial, intangible, incorporeal and without extension. If the character of the original is understood in this way, it surely follows that the soul, formed after that pattern, is recognized by the same characteristics, so that it too is immaterial, without visible form, intellectual and incorporeal. Let us consider, then, when human nature comes closer to the original beauty: while living in the flesh, or when we come to be outside it. But this is clear to everyone: just as the flesh

…being material, is fitted to this material life, so too the soul shares in the intellectual and immaterial life at the moment when it shakes off the matter that encloses it. What in all this, then, deserves to be called a misfortune? If the body were the true good, we would have reason to be distressed at being estranged from the flesh, since we would be falling away from that good, and our kinship with the good would be cast off along with the body. But the good that surpasses all thought, in whose image we were made, is intellectual and incorporeal. It follows that we should be convinced of this: when through death we pass over to the incorporeal, we draw near to that nature which is free of all bodily grossness. We strip off our covering of flesh like a hideous mask and return to our own beauty, the beauty in which we were formed at the beginning, when we were made in the image of the archetype. Such a thought should give those who hear these words reason for joy, not dejection. Once a person has fulfilled this necessary service, he no longer lives among things alien to him. He has given back to each of the elements what belongs to it, what he had borrowed from them, and has returned to the hearth that is his own by nature, the pure and incorporeal. For the matter of the body is truly something foreign and alien to the incorporeal nature, and the mind, which in this life is necessarily entangled with it, suffers hardship from sharing a life with what is not its kind. The elements are bound together like a people formed from men of different nations who speak different tongues and have strange customs. Their fellowship is forced and discordant, because each is drawn by its own nature toward what is akin and proper to it. The mind blended with these elements is uncompounded, simple and uniform in nature. It lives among strangers and aliens and has no kinship with the people of elements that surrounds it. Sown by some necessity into the many parts of the body, it does violence to its own nature by being united with things of another kind. [?] When the elements come apart from one another and are naturally drawn toward what is akin and proper to them, the natural union is necessarily loosened and split, and the senses feel pain. The thinking part of the soul sides with the senses, since habit inclines it toward whatever is causing pain at the moment. The mind therefore ceases from its distress and pain only when it comes out of the battle waged in the combination of opposing elements. Cold may be defeated by prevailing heat, or heat may flee before an excess of cold. The moist may give way to the dominance of the dry, or the firmness of the dry may be dissolved by an excess of moisture. Then, when death has ended the war within us, the mind is at peace. It has left the no-man's-land of the battle, by which I mean the body, and has come out from the array of the elements drawn up against one another. It lives by itself, and through rest it regains its strength, which had been worn down in its entanglement with the

body. These things, then, and others like them, the mind says to those who live in the body, almost giving them voice: "O men, you do not know precisely the state you are in now, and you do not yet understand what you will pass into. Reason has not yet been able to discover the nature of the present life. It looks only to the habit of living and cannot know what the nature of the body is, or the power of the senses, or the structure of the limbs and organs, or the arrangement of the inner parts, or the self-moving activity of the nerves. Nor can it know how one part of what is in us hardens into bone while another becomes the luminous radiance of the eye; how from the same food and the same drink one part is thinned into hair and another spreads out into nails at the fingertips; how the fire in the heart is kept always burning and is carried through the arteries to the whole body; or how what we drink, once it reaches the liver, changes its form and quality and turns of itself into blood through some alteration. The knowledge of all these things is still hidden from us, so that we do not understand the very life we are living. And those who live with the senses cannot see at all the life that is separated from sense. How could anyone see by the senses what lies beyond the senses? Both lives, then, are equally unknown: this one because you look only at what appears, that one because the senses cannot reach it. What has happened to you, O men? You cling to this life as good, though you do not know it, and you dread and shudder at that one as harsh and fearful, for no other reason than that you do not know what it is like." And yet there are many other things, even among those that appear to our senses, of which we are ignorant without being afraid. What is the nature of the things seen in the heavens? What drives the heavenly sphere round in its contrary motion? What holds the earth firm? How does the flowing nature of the waters keep coming out of the earth without the earth being used up? We do not know many such things, and we do not judge our ignorance of them a reason for fear. Indeed, we believe that the nature which surpasses every mind exists, the divine, blessed and incomprehensible nature. Yet no one has found by conjecture any understanding of what its being consists in. Even so, we love what is unknown with our whole heart and soul and strength, though our reasonings cannot grasp it. Why, then, does this irrational fear arise, as if the life awaiting us after this one were painful? We fear what we do not know purely because we do not know it, just as infants are frightened by groundless imaginings. Whoever wishes to see the truth of things first forms a notion of the matter and then considers what it is like by nature, whether it is useful and approachable or harsh and to be shunned. But how could anyone with sense judge something wholly obscure and unknown to be harsh, suspecting the mere departure from habit

of being some attack of fire or of a wild beast? And yet life clearly teaches us not always to look to habit, but always to turn our desires toward what is good. Life in the womb does not last forever for those being formed there. As long as they are inside the womb, nature makes life in the belly pleasant and suitable for them. Once they have come out, they do not stay at the breast forever either, but only as long as this is good and suitable for the immaturity of their age. After that they pass on to another stage of life, and habit does not persuade them to stay at the breast. Then, after infancy, come the pursuits of youths and later those of riper years, and a person passes through them in sequence, painlessly changing his habits along with his age. If the child nourished in its mother's womb had a voice, it would be indignant at being turned out of the womb by birth and would cry out that it was suffering terribly at being torn from its pleasant way of life. This is in fact what it does, shedding tears with its first breath at birth, as though indignant and lamenting its separation from its accustomed life. In the same way, it seems to me, those who are distressed at the change from the present life suffer what embryos suffer, since they want to live forever in [?] this material unpleasantness. When the birth pangs of death deliver people into another life, those who pass into that light and breathe the pure air learn by experience how great the difference is between that life and this one. But those left behind in this wet and soggy life, who are simply embryos and not yet men, pity the one who has gone out before them from the confinement that encloses us, as though he had lost some good. They do not know that, as with a newborn baby, the eye is opened when it comes out of what now confines it. (We must of course understand this as the eye of the soul, by which it discerns the truth of things.) The organ of hearing is opened too, and through it the soul hears unspeakable words, which a man may not utter, as the Apostle says. The mouth is opened, and it draws in the pure and immaterial spirit, by which it is strengthened for the intelligible voice and the true word, when it joins its sound to that of the saints keeping festival in their choir. In the same way the soul is granted a divine taste, through which it knows, as the psalm says, that the Lord is good. Through the sense of smell it perceives the fragrance of Christ. And it gains the power of touch, touching the truth and handling the Word, according to the testimony of John. If these and similar things are laid up for people after their birth through death, what is the point of grief and gloom and dejection? Now let anyone who looks at the nature of things

answer us. Does he think it better to be led astray by the bodily senses in judging what is good than to look with the naked eye of the soul at the very truth of things? Here the soul is under a kind of compulsion to be enslaved to someone else's judgment in forming its idea of the good. The full power of the soul cannot be contained in the body of an infant, while the activity of the senses is born complete together with the baby. For this reason sense gets ahead of the understanding in judging the good. Whatever has already appeared to the senses and been taken as good, and has been fixed beforehand by habit, the soul accepts without examination, convinced that whatever the senses have testified to first is good. So it sees the good in colours and flavours and such trifles. But when these no longer appear, after the departure from the body, the true good, to which the soul is akin by nature, must necessarily appear to it. Sight will no longer be lured by fine colour, since this eye will no longer exist. Nor will the scale of choice tip toward anything else that sweetens the senses, since all bodily sensation will have been extinguished. Only the activity of the intellect will remain, touching the intelligible beauty in an immaterial and incorporeal way, and nature will receive back its own good without hindrance. That good is neither colour, nor shape, nor extension, nor size, but surpasses everything we can conjecture or imagine. "What then?" someone who is displeased with the present life may say. "What is the body for, and why do we have it, if the argument has shown that life without it is better?" We shall reply that the gain from these things is not small for those who are able to look at the whole economy of nature. The life of the angels is truly blessed, since it needs nothing of the weight of the body. Yet this life too contributes something toward that one, for the present life becomes the road to what we hope for. One can see this in plants. The fruit begins from the flower and proceeds through it to becoming fruit, although the flower is not the fruit. Likewise the crops that spring up from seeds do not appear at once as ears of grain. The first shoot is grass. Then a stalk forms from it as the grass withers around it, and so the grain ripens in the head of the ear. Yet the farmer does not find fault with this necessary cycle and sequence. He does not say, "Why a flower before the fruit? What is the grass for that springs up first from the seed, if the flower falls off and the grass withers in vain, contributing nothing to human food?" For whoever looks at the wonder-working of nature knows that the fruit could not be brought to perfection from seeds and shoots in any other way, unless this skilful sequence prepared the way for its completion. The grass sent up first from the seeds is useless for our enjoyment, but that does not make what happens superfluous and pointless. The one who needs

food looks to his own need, but the principle of nature looks to nothing else than how it may bring the bearing of fruit to completion through the appointed sequence. So first the plant grows into the ground beneath it through many roots, and through these it draws in moisture and the nourishment suited to it. Then it sprouts grass, making the green growth a covering for the root against harm from the air. This is not the fruit, but it is a kind of helper and road toward the fruit's completion. First, it purges the power lying in the seed, since nature clears away the grass beforehand like a residue of the fruit. Then it becomes a shelter for the root against the harms that come from the air through frost and heat. When the seed has been established more firmly in the depths of its roots, the grass is neglected, because the root no longer needs the covering, and all the plant's power is given to the shooting up of the stalk. With a kind of engineering wisdom, nature skilfully builds its pipe-like structure. The stalk grows straight up and is divided at intervals by sheaths wrapped one over another all around it. At first the stalk is moist and weak, and it must be nurtured inside these sheaths and girded for safety by the joints in between. When it has shot up to its proper height, the stalk puts out its head, as the last sheath reveals the ear from within itself. The ear divides like hair into many awns, and it hides its grain, which is nourished in the husks at the base of the awns. The farmer is not displeased with the roots of the seeds, or with the grass that comes up first from the seed, or with the awns of the ear. In each of these he sees some necessary use, by which nature skilfully makes its way and leads the fruit to perfection, purifying its fertile power by discarding what is useless. If that is so, it is time for you too to stop being displeased that our nature advances by necessary roads to its proper end. Consider instead, by analogy with seeds, that whatever is present at any given time serves some useful and necessary purpose, yet is not the thing for whose sake we came into being. We were not brought into existence by our Creator in order to be embryos. Nature's aim does not look to the life of an infant, or to the successive ages of life, which it keeps putting on one after another, changing its form with time. Nor does it look to the dissolution that comes upon the body through death. All these and similar things are parts of the road we travel. The goal and end of the journey through them is the restoration to our original state, which is nothing other than likeness to the Divine. In the image of the ear of grain, nature's reason showed that the grass sent up first was necessary. Yet farming is not done for its sake, and sheaths, awns, stalk and joints are not what the farmer's labour aims at. It aims at the nourishing grain that advances through them to perfection. So too the expected

end of life is blessedness. Everything we now see happening to the body, whether death, old age, youth, infancy or formation in the womb, is like the grass, the awns and the stalks. All of it is the road, the sequence and the means toward the perfection we hope for. If you are wise and keep your eyes on that perfection, you will not be hostile to these things. Nor will you be attached to them with passion and desire, so as either to grieve at being parted from them or to desert to death. It may be worth adding this to the argument, even if it seems out of sequence: nature is constantly rehearsing death, and death is bound up with life as life advances through time. Life always moves from the past toward the future and never turns back, so death is what always follows close behind the activity of life. In the time that has passed, all vital motion and activity has entirely ceased. Inactivity and inertness are proper to death, and this always follows behind the activity of life. So it is not beyond the truth to say that death is interwoven with this life. One may also find this idea confirmed in another way, with experience itself bearing witness to the doctrine. The man of today is not the same as the man of yesterday in his material substance. Something of him is constantly dying, stinking, decaying and being cast out, as nature carries the deathly stench out of the body's structure as if out of a house and hands over to the earth whatever has already passed beyond the life-giving power. Therefore, in the words of the great Paul, we die daily. We do not remain always the same in the same house of the body. Through addition and discharge we become someone different each time, as though continually being changed into a new body. Why then are we astonished at death, when life in the flesh has been shown to be a constant practice and training for it? If you speak of sleep and waking, you speak of another way in which death is interwoven with life. In those who sleep, sense is extinguished, and waking enacts in us once again the resurrection we hope for. But what was set before us has not yet been made clear by what has been said, because the digression led the argument off to another subject. Let us then take up again what was proposed: the nature of the body too is not without use for our expected hope of good things. If we were what we were made at the beginning, we would surely not have needed the garment of skin, since the likeness to the Divine would shine upon us. The divine stamp that appeared in us at the beginning was not a property of some particular shape or colour. Man was adorned with the very things in which the divine beauty is seen, imitating the archetypal grace through freedom from passion, blessedness and incorruption. But through the deceit of the enemy of our life, man voluntarily inclined toward what is beastly and irrational. To make him withdraw from the

worse against his will and transfer him to the better by compulsion seems useful to those who do not examine the matter. But to the Fashioner of our nature it appeared unprofitable and unjust, since such a dispensation would inflict on nature the loss of the greatest of goods. Man was made godlike and blessed, and was honoured with free will, for self-rule and having no master are proper to divine blessedness. To force him toward anything by necessity would therefore have been to take away his dignity. Human nature had rushed voluntarily, by its own free movement, toward something it ought not to have. If God had forcibly and by compulsion drawn it away from what it had chosen, that would have taken away its preeminent good and deprived it of its godlike honour, for free will is godlike. So that nature might keep its freedom and evil might still be removed, the wisdom of God found this device: to let man go where he wished, so that he might taste the evils he desired and learn by experience what he had exchanged for what. Then, by his own desire, he would run back voluntarily to the first blessedness, having cast off from his nature like a burden everything passionate and irrational. He would be purified either in the present life through prayer and philosophy, or after his departure from here through the smelting of the purifying fire. Imagine a physician who by his art has full knowledge of both remedies and poisons. He gives a young man sound advice, but his advice cannot restrain someone immature in years and judgment who has set his heart on some deadly fruit or herb. Having every kind of antidote ready, he lets the boy partake of what will harm him. In this way the boy learns through painful experience how useful his father's advice was and comes to long for health. The physician then uses the antidotes to bring him back to the good condition he lost through his absurd desire for poisons. In the same way the sweet and good Father of our nature, who also knows the means by which we are saved, made the poison known to man and advised him not to partake of it. When the desire for the worse prevailed, He was not at a loss for good antidotes by which to bring man back again to the health he had at the beginning. Man preferred this material pleasure to the joy of the soul. In a way, God seemed to go along with his impulse through the garment of skin, which He put on him because of his inclination toward the worse. Through it the properties of irrational nature were mingled with man. From irrational animals a garment was made for the rational nature by the wisdom of Him who arranges what is better through its opposites. The garment of skin carries in itself all the properties that belonged to irrational nature: pleasure and anger, gluttony and greed, and the like. It gives the human will a path to incline either way, and it becomes material for both virtue and vice. For while man lives among these things in this present life,

…by its own free movement. If it marks off what belongs to it from what is irrational, and turns its gaze on itself by living a more refined life, it will make this present life a purification of the evil that has been mixed into it, mastering irrationality by reason. But if it leans toward the irrational pull of the passions, and makes the skin of the irrational animals its accomplice in them, it will take a different and better counsel later, after its departure from the body. Then it will learn how virtue differs from vice, because it cannot share in the divine nature until the purifying fire has cleansed away the filth mixed into the soul. These are the reasons that made the body necessary for us. Through it our free will is preserved, and our return to the good is not prevented. In this cycle our turning toward the better comes about freely. Some achieve the spiritual life, free from passion, already here in the flesh. We hear that the patriarchs and the prophets were like this, and those who were with them and came after them and rose to perfection through virtue and philosophy: I mean the disciples, the apostles and the martyrs, and all who valued the virtuous life above the material one. Even if they are fewer than the crowd that slides away toward the worse, they still stand as witnesses that virtue can be achieved in the flesh. The rest, through the treatment that comes later in the purifying fire, cast off their passionate attachment to matter. Through desire for good things they return freely to the grace that was given to nature from the beginning. For the desire for what is alien does not stay in nature forever. Whatever is not one's own, whatever nature had no share in from the beginning, soon fills and cloys. Only what is kindred and of the same kind remains forever longed for and loved, as long as nature stays undistorted in itself. But if it suffers some distortion through a wicked choice, then desire for alien things arises in it. Enjoying them pleases not the nature but the passion of the nature. When the passion departs, the desire for what is contrary to nature departs with it, and nature again longs for what is its own and suits it. This is what is pure, immaterial and incorporeal, and no one would be wrong to call it proper to the Godhead that transcends all things. Consider the bodily eyes. When some sharp humour clouds the visual spirit, darkness becomes more pleasant, because thickness is akin to darkness. But if some treatment consumes whatever was troubling the spirit, light becomes familiar and suitable again, mingling with the pure, radiant pupil. In the same way, vice flowed like a humour over the soul's power of sight through the deceit of the Adversary. Reason then turned willingly toward the life of darkness and became at home in the gloom through passion. For everyone

who does evil hates the light, as the divine voice says. But when evil has been used up and removed from existing things, and has gone back into non-being, nature looks up to the light again with pleasure, because what clouded the purity of the soul has gone. What has been said therefore shows that it is pointless to be hostile to the nature of the flesh. The cause of evils does not depend on it. If it did, evil would hold equal power over everyone who has been given bodily life. But each of those remembered for virtue lived in the flesh and was not in vice. This makes it clear that the body is not the cause of the passions. The cause is the choice that creates the passions. The body moves in keeping with its own nature, toward the things that maintain its constitution and keep it in being, and its own impulses steer it toward them. For example, it needs food and drink, so that the strength it has breathed away can be brought back in to replace what is lacking, and appetite moves toward this. Again, mortal though it is, the nature of the body is made immortal through the succession of offspring, and so it is suitably disposed toward this impulse too. Moreover, the body was made bare of any covering of hair, and for this reason we needed clothing from outside. And since we could not withstand scorching heat, cold and rain, we sought the shelter of houses. The person who looks at these and similar things sensibly, with need in view, accepts each of them calmly and makes need the goal of desire: a house, a garment, marriage, food. Through each of these he supplies what nature lacks. But the servant of pleasures has turned these necessary needs into roads for the passions. Instead of food he seeks luxury. Instead of clothing he chooses finery. Instead of the houses he needs, he wants extravagance. Instead of having children, he looks to lawless and forbidden pleasures. That is why greed has come reveling into human life through wide gates, together with softness, pride, vanity and every kind of dissipation. These and similar things have sprouted beside the necessary needs like suckers and dry shoots, because desire has gone beyond the limits of need and spread itself over pursuits that serve no useful purpose. What does engraved silver, decked with gold and gems, have to do with the usefulness of food? Why should a garment need gold thread, bright purple, and woven pictures, in which weavers depict wars, wild beasts and the like on tunics and robes? The disease of greed grew up as an ally of all this. To get the means and the money for these things, people obtain the materials of their desires through greed. And

greed opened the way for insatiability [?]. In the words of Solomon this is the leaking jar, always running short for those who draw from it and always found empty. So it is not the body that produces the occasions of evil but the choice, which twists the purpose of need into a desire for improper things. Let the thoughtless, then, stop maligning the body. Later, when it has been transformed into something more divine through the regeneration, the soul will be adorned with it, after death has cleansed away whatever is superfluous and useless for enjoying the life to come. The things our body is now suited for will not be the same things that serve it in the later life. The make-up of our body will instead be proper and suited to the enjoyment of that life, fittingly arranged for sharing in good things. Let me give an example, since it is better to make the thought clear by something familiar. A lump of iron serves the smith's craft, acting as an unwrought anvil for the craftsman. But when the iron has to be reworked into something finer, the fire carefully purges the lump, and it sheds everything earthy and useless, which those who practise this craft call slag. In this way what was once an anvil is finely worked and becomes a breastplate or some other delicate piece, purged of that waste by smelting. Yet as long as it was an anvil, the slag was not thought of as waste for the use it then served, for the slag mixed into the lump added something to the bulk of the iron. We have now understood the example. Next we must carry the idea seen in it over to the subject in hand. What is it, then? The nature of the body now has many slag-like qualities. In the present life they contribute to something useful, but they are entirely useless and alien to the blessedness we expect hereafter. What happens to iron in the fire, when smelting removes everything useless, death accomplishes for the body, removing all waste through the dissolution that comes in death. Those who have thought about it already know well enough what the body is later cleansed of. If these things were missing in the present life, this life would suffer for it. Still, for the sake of clarity, we too will say it briefly. Suppose, for the sake of argument, that the lump stands for the desire that is naturally at work in everyone. The slag stands for the things desire now strives toward: pleasures, riches, love of glory, power, fits of anger, vanities and the like. Death becomes an exact purification of all these and things like them. Stripped and cleansed of them all, desire will turn its activity toward the only thing that is truly desirable, longed for and lovely. It will not quench

altogether the impulses naturally implanted in us toward such things. It will transform them toward an immaterial sharing in good things. For there is the love of true beauty, which never ceases. There is the praiseworthy greed for the treasures of wisdom, and the fine and good love of glory that is achieved by sharing in the kingdom of God. There is the fine passion of insatiability, whose good longing is never cut short by having its fill of the things above. A person who has learned this knows that at the appointed times the Craftsman of the universe will reforge the lump of the body into a weapon of honour, fashioning a breastplate of righteousness, as the Apostle says, a sword of the Spirit, a helmet of hope, and the whole armour of God. Such a person therefore loves his own body, according to the law of the Apostle, who says, "No one ever hated his own body." But it is the purified body that should be loved, not the slag that is being discarded. For it is true, as the divine voice says, that if our earthly house, this tent, is dissolved, then we shall find it to be a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens, worthy to be God's dwelling place in the Spirit. And let no one sketch for me the features, shape and form of that house not made with hands on the model of the features we now show, which set us apart from one another by their peculiarities. The divine oracles proclaim the resurrection to us, and divine Scripture also assures us that those renewed through the resurrection must be changed. It follows that what we shall be changed into must be entirely hidden and unknown, since no example of what we hope for can be seen in the present life. Now everything thick and solid naturally tends downward. But then the body will be transformed so as to tend upward. The word says that, after nature has been changed in all who have come back to life through the resurrection, "We shall be caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord." In those who are changed, then, weight does not remain in the body, and those transformed into the more divine state rise aloft together with the incorporeal nature. If so, the body's other properties are surely changed into something more divine as well: colour, shape, outline, and every detail. For this reason we see no need for those changed through the resurrection to show the kind of difference that nature now necessarily has for the sake of the succession of offspring. Yet we cannot clearly declare that it will not exist either, since we do not know what these things will pass into through the change. But we do not doubt that all will be of one kind when we all become one body of Christ, formed by the one character, with the divine image shining equally on all. As for what will be given us in place of such properties when our nature is changed, we declare that it lies beyond

all conjecture. But so that our discussion of this question is not left wholly untried, we say this. The distinction between male and female serves nature for nothing except the bearing of children. So perhaps, in discussing this, one may form a conjecture worthy of God's promised blessing of good things: that nature's power of generation will pass over into the service of that birth which the great Isaiah shared in when he said, "Through fear of you, O Lord, we conceived in the womb, we were in labour and gave birth; we have brought forth the spirit of your salvation upon the earth." For if such a birth is good, and childbearing becomes a cause of salvation, as the Apostle says, then whoever begets the spirit of salvation never stops. Through such a birth he has once and for all borne for himself an abundance of good things. Suppose someone says that the features which now shape us will be with us again when we come back to life. Our mind is not ready to suppose either that it is so or that it is not. If someone says that we will return to life in the same form, the argument falls into great difficulty. A person does not always stay the same in the form of his features, because age and illness reshape him from one form to another. The infant and the youngster are shaped one way, and the boy, the man, the middle-aged, the elderly and the old man each another way. None of these resembles any other. Then there are the one discoloured by jaundice and the one swollen with dropsy, the one wasted by consumption and the one grown fat from some imbalance of the humours, the bilious, the sanguine and the phlegmatic, each shaped to match whichever imbalance prevails. It would not be right to think that these conditions remain after the return to life, since the change makes everything ready for something more divine. Nor is it easy to work out what sort of form will bloom on us, since we believe that the good things set before us in hope are beyond eye and ear and thought. Perhaps someone who said that the particular character of each person's moral qualities is what will identify each one would not be entirely wrong. Now some variation in the elements within us produces the differences of features in each person. The particular form is shaped and coloured by an excess or a deficiency of one or other of the corresponding elements. In the same way, it seems to me, what will then give each person his form will not be these elements but the properties of vice or virtue. Their particular blend with one another will mark the form one way or another. Something like this happens even in the present life, when the outward look of the face reveals the hidden state of the soul. This is how we easily recognize the one gripped by grief, the one stirred up by anger, and the one melting with desire. Likewise, at the other extreme, we recognize the cheerful, the one free from anger, and the one adorned with the dignified character of temperance.

[?] …grace, so that each one gives back the same gladness to his neighbour. Through these qualities each one rejoices at seeing the other's beauty and gladdens the other in return, since no vice distorts anyone's form into an ugly character. Our mind has discussed these things for us on behalf of the departed, playing their parts as best we could. Let us now end our counsel to those in deep mourning with the words of the great Paul: "I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, about those who have fallen asleep, so that you may not grieve as the rest do, who have no hope." If, then, our discourse has philosophized about those who have fallen asleep and we have learned from it something worth our serious attention, let us no longer give way to this ignoble and slavish grief. If we must grieve, let us choose the grief that is praiseworthy and virtuous. Pleasure has one kind that is brutish and irrational and another that is pure and immaterial. In the same way the opposite of pleasure is divided into vice and virtue. There is, then, a kind of mourning that is called blessed and is not useless for acquiring virtue, and it is the opposite of this irrational and slavish dejection. Someone who has given way to dejection will reproach himself afterwards with regret, as one who was carried out of his settled state when the passion got the better of him. But blessed mourning brings a sadness that leaves no regret and no shame for those who achieve the virtuous life through it.

For a person truly mourns when he becomes aware of the good things from which he has fallen. He sets this perishable and soiled life against that pure blessedness which was in his power before he misused his power for evil. The more heavily his mourning over such a life weighs on him, the sooner he gains the good things he longs for. Awareness of the good he has lost kindles his zeal for what he longs for. Since, as the discourse has shown, there is also a mourning that saves, listen, you who are easily dragged down into the passion of grief. We do not forbid grief, but we counsel the good kind in place of the condemned kind. So do not grieve with the grief of the world, which produces death, as the Apostle says, but with godly grief, whose end is the salvation of the soul. The tear shed idly and in vain over those who have fallen asleep may even become a cause of condemnation for one who badly manages what is meant to be useful. He who made all things in wisdom built this capacity for grief into nature for a purpose: to purify the vice that had already taken hold, and to equip us for sharing in the good things we hope for. If so, the one who sheds tears in vain and to no purpose may perhaps be accused before his own master, as the Gospel says, as a bad steward who uselessly squanders the wealth entrusted to him. Everything that serves the good is wealth and is counted among the precious treasures. "I do not want you, then, to be ignorant, brothers, about those who have fallen asleep": this is what we have learned, along with any further teaching that the Holy Spirit reveals to the more perfect, "so that you may not grieve as the rest do, who have no hope." It belongs to unbelievers alone to confine the hope of living to the present life, and so they count death a calamity, because they do not hope for what we believe. But we have believed in the great guarantor of the resurrection from the dead, the Master of all creation himself. He died and rose for this very reason, to confirm by his deed the word about the resurrection. Let us therefore hold without doubt to the hope of good things, and while that hope is with us, grief over the departed will have no place. May our God and Lord Jesus Christ, who comforts the lowly, comfort your hearts and strengthen them in his love through his compassion, for to him be glory to the ages of ages. Amen.
